documents.abstract: This research examines the effectiveness of artificial intelligence as a cybersecurity support tool for nontechnical users. The study evaluated ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude 3 across five simulated cybersecurity scenarios involving phishing attempts, password reuse, fraudulent online stores, and suspicious security alerts. Using a standardized rubric, the study compared each model's threat recognition, safety recommendations, cybersecurity knowledge, clarity, and reliability. The findings highlight conversational AI's potential to improve cybersecurity awareness while also showing limitations in the accuracy, accessibility, and reliability of AI-generated security advice. The study emphasizes the importance of independent verification and human judgment when using AI to navigate online threats.

Abstract This theoretical article examines artificial intelligence in organizational digitalization. It distinguishes digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation, then combines sociotechnical theory with the dynamic capabilities perspective to explain how technology interacts with employees, routines, organizational structures and adaptation. The framework proposes that artificial intelligence supports transformation when aligned with strategy, integrated into processes and complemented by employee expertise, data and responsible governance. It highlights tensions involving discretion, bias, accountability and the fit between standardized systems and local practices. The article contributes propositions for empirical research and argues that AI’s value depends on integrating technical systems with human capabilities and organizational oversight. AI applications can automate repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, personalize services and support decisions. However, their effects depend on data quality, employee skills, leadership commitment and the organizational context. For this reason, the article moves the focus beyond the simple adoption of AI and highlights the organizational capabilities and governance needed to integrate it responsibly. Keywords: artificial intelligence; organizational digitalization; digital transformation; dynamic capabilities; sociotechnical systems; AI adoption; responsible AI governance.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) does not constitute a single phenomenon in archival practice. It may generate potential records, support archival functions, assist tool development, analyze holdings, become an object of preservation, or mediate access. Treating these different modes of involvement as homogeneous produces imprecise diagnoses and inadequate safeguards. This theoretical-conceptual article proposes a six-mode model: AI-assisted record production, AI tools for archival functions, AI-assisted tool development, AI analysis of archival holdings, AI systems as preservation objects, and AI-mediated access. Each mode is evaluated against common requirements of archival trust — authenticity, reliability, accuracy, and the chain of preservation — and is subject to a cross-cutting governance framework based on paradata, explainable AI, bias mitigation, ethical use, and accountable human oversight. The analysis is guided by the theoretical-methodological framework of InterPARES, particularly InterPARES Trust AI (2021–2026). The article concludes that AI can support archival work only when its use is governed by archival principles, documented procedures, and clearly assigned human and institutional responsibility. The model provides an instrument for analyzing AI initiatives, designing safeguards, and guiding future empirical validation through case studies.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in education to support learning, teaching, assessm ent, and academ ic adm inistration. Exam ples include adaptive learning system s, intelligent tutoring tools, autom ated feedback, learning analytics, and generative AI assistants. This paper review s selected published research and international guidance to exam ine the potential benefits, m ajor risks, and future directions of AI in education. The literature indicates that AI can support personalized learning, provide tim ely feedback, assist educators w ith planning, and im prove access to learning support. A t the sam e tim e, its use raises concerns about privacy, bias, accuracy, unequal access, academ ic integrity, and over-reliance on autom ated system s. documents.abstract: Purpose This study addresses the following research question: What are the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) for Personalized Learning and Online Higher Education (OHE)? Design/methodology/approach A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews including faculty members and higher education administrators. The data were analyzed to identify the adoption factors, challenges, opportunities, and ethical considerations. An Integrative Model of Adopting AI in Online Higher Education (IMAOHE) was developed based on the empirical findings. Findings AI supports personalized learning through adaptive assessment, real-time feedback, learning analytics, and tailored content. The reported challenges include ethical dilemmas, institutional barriers, and the need to preserve teacher autonomy. Research limitations/implications Limited respondents and lack of student perspectives suggest future research with larger, more diverse samples and mixed-methods or longitudinal designs. Practical implications The model guides institutions, educators, and developers to integrate AI ethically and strategically, ensuring meaningful, context-aware learning. Social implications AI can enhance equity, inclusion, and student-centered learning while maintaining human mediation and cultural sensitivity. Originality/value This study provides an empirically grounded model linking AI adoption to pedagogical personalization in OHE, offering actionable insights for ethical and effective AI integration.

documents.abstract: This repository contains the supplementary data and materials supporting the systematic review entitled “Artificial Intelligence in Higher Mathematics Education: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Informed Framework for Productive Pedagogical Integration and Human–AI Interaction” by Felix O. Egara and Alfred M. Msomi. The review synthesises empirical research published between January 2021 and September 2026 on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher mathematics education. Searches were conducted in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection, and 18 studies meeting the eligibility criteria were included in the review. The repository contains the original database search exports, the merged bibliographic dataset, the PRISMA 2020 reporting checklist, the full search strategies and eligibility criteria, the evidence-to-framework synthesis matrix, and the study characteristics and data-extraction matrix. These materials document the review’s information sources, study selection, data extraction, and evidence synthesis. They are intended to support transparency, methodological reporting, and further scholarly engagement with research on AI-supported mathematics learning in higher education.

documents.abstract: Background:AI is being increasingly investigated as a clinical decision support tool for ED triage and acute-care prioritization. Machine-learning, deep-learning, natural language processing (NLP) and large language model systems have shown good predictive performance but concerns remain about under-triage, over-triage, generalizability, workflow integration and implementation safety. We systematically reviewed the accuracy, safety and implementation readiness of AI-driven clinical decision-support systems for ED triage.Methods:This review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane Library were searched (citation chaining, reference-list screening and recent systematic reviews were also used). Of the 1076 records identified, 312 duplicates were removed and 764 records screened; 79 full-text reports were assessed and 65 excluded; fourteen studies were included in narrative synthesis. Meta-analysis was not performed because populations, AI architectures, triage systems, reference standards and outcome metrics are highly heterogeneous.Results:Conventional machine learning, gradient boosting, neural networks, deep learning, natural language processing and large language models were included in the studies. AI systems generally outperformed conventional triage for critical illness prediction (hospitalization), intensive-care admission and mortality; reported AUROCs for early mortality were 0.962 and for 30-day mortality 0.925. Direct triage systems also had some success: KATE had 75.7% ESI assignment accuracy; prospective GPT-4 and GPT-4o studieshad κ = 0.899 and multicenter κ = 0.833 with F1 = 0.897 agreement with expert triage but safety outcomes under-triage/over-triage subgroup performance and patient-important outcomes were inconsistently reported.Conclusions:ED triage systems powered by AI have great potential as supervised clinical decision support tools but not yet enough evidence to justify autonomous deployment. Prospective multicenter validation, standardized safety metrics, subgroup analysis, workflow evaluation, governance and post-deployment monitoring are needed before widespread implementation

documents.abstract: Description / Abstract Title: Safeguarding Trust in AI-Assisted Credit Scoring in Indian Digital Lending: A Documentary Analysis of the RBI’s 2025 Directions Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and alternative data increasingly inform digital credit decisions, raising critical questions about privacy, fairness, decision transparency, and accountability. In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued the Digital Lending Directions, 2025 on 8 May 2025. This study examines these Directions as a dated regulatory instrument and assesses their coverage of trust-related safeguards. Reviewing the 2025 framework alongside earlier Indian digital-lending instruments, the study applies a five-part analytical framework developed from the literature: decision transparency, privacy and data minimisation, fairness, human recourse, and model governance. It also compares the Indian framework with international guidance from the European Banking Authority (EBA, 2020), the OECD (2021), and the US NIST (2023). The documentary analysis reveals that while the RBI framework provides robust coverage of lender conduct, data consent, disclosures (such as the Key Facts Statement with all-in APR), and grievance redress, it exhibits notable gaps regarding mandatory pre-deployment fairness testing, ongoing model-drift monitoring, and standardised explanations for AI-assisted adverse decisions. To bridge these gaps, the study proposes a layered set of safeguards: privacy-by-design, standardised reason codes for adverse decisions, accessible routes to human review, and periodic fairness and drift audits.

documents.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly asked to reason over a user's own web traces: group chats, community threads, activity logs and revision histories. On CL-bench Life, a benchmark of such real-life context learning, frontier LLMs solve fewer than one task in five. We find that the request is not the specification: over 80% of the benchmark's rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request, as for a rule set two turns earlier or every record that meets the user's criterion, and LLMs answering directly pass only 67% of these implicit rubrics against 81% of the others. We propose QERA, a Question-driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture that asks before it answers. QERA first turns the request into a requirement checklist and typed information needs, filtered by code for faithfulness to the user's words; it then answers from the whole conversation, asks the same questions again with quotes verified by code, and applies a guarded local repair. It needs no training or rubrics and makes about four LLM calls per task. On all 405 tasks with four frontier LLMs, QERA attains the highest solving rate on every LLM (21.0% on average, against 18.2% for the strongest of three inference-time baselines and 14.6% for direct answering) and leads every baseline significantly when pooled across LLMs, while using fewer tokens than PSCI and 4-5% of the tokens of Ctx2Skill. Ablations on GPT-6-Luna show that the gain is settled before the answer, by a fixed answer protocol (+3.8 rubric points) and the request-specific questions (+1.6), and that it is concentrated on implicit rubrics, with checking afterwards refining mainly numeric requirements.

Abstract Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems are able to generate, revise and comment on second language (L2) student writing. However, less is known about where L2 writing teachers locate the opportunities and risks of such systems across the writing process. To that end, this study examined how English for academic purposes (EAP) writing instructors at two universities in Oman position GenAI within the L2 writing process. It focused on, first, the stages at which instructors locate GenAI's opportunities and risks, second, their views on GenAI as a source of feedback, and lastly their preparedness to manage academic integrity in AI-assisted L2 writing. A cross-sectional questionnaire combining Likert-scale items and open-ended prompts was completed by 51 EAP instructors , of whom 49 were retained for analysis. Closed items were analysed with descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, McNemar tests and Mann–Whitney U tests. Open-ended responses were coded by writing stage through qualitative content analysis. The results showed that L2 writing instructors located GenAI's opportunities mainly in their own preparation of materials and model texts and in feedback. On the other hand, they highlighted its risks in students' drafting and in assessment. Revising and editing was contested, cited equally often as an opportunity and a risk. EAP instructors were more confident in using GenAI to prepare materials than in designing students' use of it at each writing stage. Just over half agreed that AI improves their feedback. This view was related to their overall attitude towards GenAI but not to their confidence as feedback providers. Most instructors felt responsible for checking students' GenAI use and confident in setting boundaries, but their confidence in maintaining academic integrity was unrelated to this sense of responsibility. More EAP instructors reported knowing how to use AI detectors than understanding how such detectors work. The study concludes that EAP instructors' readiness to integrate GenAI into L2 writing teaching and learning is uneven across the L2 writing process. Professional learning and development should therefore target the pedagogical design of student-facing AI use, the evaluation of AI feedback, AI detection literacy, and L2 writing assessment redesign.

Abstract Background Artificial intelligence chatbots (AICs) are increasingly being considered for use in scholarly peer review to assist with tasks such as identifying methodological issues, verifying references, and improving language clarity. However, concerns remain regarding their reliability, ethical implications, and transparency. Evidence on how medical journal peer reviewers perceive the role and impact of AICs is limited. This study explored reviewers’ familiarity with AICs, perceived benefits and challenges, ethical concerns, and anticipated future roles in peer review. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of medical journal peer reviewers. Corresponding author information was extracted from MEDLINE-indexed articles added to PubMed within a six-week period. A total of 72,851 authors were invited via email to participate; those who self-identified as peer reviewers were eligible. The 29-item survey assessed familiarity with AICs and perceptions of their benefits and limitations in peer review. The survey was administered via SurveyMonkey from April 28 to June 16, 2025, with two reminder emails sent during the data collection period. Results Of 66,679 email invitations, a total of 1260 respondents provided survey responses (response rate: 1.9%), of whom 1157 met the eligibility criteria, and 1077 answered the main survey questions. Most participants were familiar with AICs (86.2%) and had used them for general purposes (87.7%), though most report not using AICs for peer review purposes (70.3%). Most respondents reported that their institutions do not provide training on AIC use in peer review (69.5%), although many expressed interest in such training (60.7%). Perceptions of AIC benefits were mixed, while concerns were widely shared, particularly regarding potential algorithmic bias (80.3%) and issues related to trust and user acceptance (73.3%). Conclusions While familiarity with AICs is high among medical journal peer reviewers, their reported use in peer review remains limited. There is clear interest in training and guidance, however, concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and research integrity persist and should be addressed before broader implementation.

documents.abstract: AbstractThis article explores the concept of Cognitive Surrender in AI-Driven Ergonomics — the risk that as AI becomes more competent in safety, human judgment is outsourced. Drawing on 27 years of EHS experience in Brazil (SP, GO, RJ, MS) managing Safety, Fire Protection and Road Safety in sugar-ethanol plants, soybean processing and construction, and now building EkoSeg EHS US LLC in Salt Lake City, UT, the author argues for AI for Augmentation, not Automation. The study bridges Brazil's NR-17 Ergonomic Work Analysis (AET) and OSHA's MSD prevention, analyzing the emergence of computer vision solutions like Kinebot (Curitiba), validated by Marfrig, P&G, Electrolux, with R$3M investment in Feb 2026 for global expansion. Kinebot delivers 5x faster and 80% cheaper analysis via phone video. The author presents lessons from the 62nd NISO Conference, Killarney, Ireland (2026): dashboards (Power BI integrating Safety Observations, NC, OFI, Near Miss, Training Expiry) don't save lives alone; conversations do. A framework is proposed: (a) Keep the Worker in the Loop — every AI high-risk flag (RULA 7) must trigger a Gemba walk, (b) Use Leading Indicators — % stations analyzed by AI, training validity, (c) Bridge NR-17 and OSHA. Author: Jailton da Silva, EHS Manager, 27 Years in HSE, Founder EkoSeg EHS US LLC & EkoSeg Segurança e Meio Ambiente, Brazil to Utah. Keywords: Cognitive Surrender, AI-Driven Ergonomics, NR-17, OSHA, RULA, REBA, Kinebot, EHS, Power BI, EkoSeg

documents.abstract: People routinely form expectations about how others will behave in morally difficult situations, and such expectations guide consequential decisions, including whom to trust, hire, or delegate responsibility to. The present research examined whether baby-schema-related cues systematically bias these moral predictions. Across three experiments with Chinese university students (total N = 858), we tested three manifestations of baby-schema-related cues that share the function of evoking infant-like associations: repeated two-syllable names (Experiment 1), babyfaced appearance (Experiment 2), and visually cute artificial intelligence (AI) avatar designs (Experiment 3). Participants consistently perceived decision-makers displaying baby-schema-related cues as less likely to make utilitarian choices involving direct harm to others. The results show that superficially irrelevant social cues can bias moral expectations about others, although the underlying psychological mechanism remains to be clarified. These findings are relevant to moral psychology, person perception, and the design and evaluation of AI systems.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: Users are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, allowing agents to perform long-running, multi-step workflows on their behalf. However, agents may perform these tasks in ways that depart from users' expectations for how they should be carried out, leading to what we call agentic delegation failures. We leverage a large corpus of 163,487 Reddit posts, describing AI agent use, to develop MANDATE: a taxonomy of 23 failure categories organized into seven groups. A follow-up study with 73 AI agent users examined the relationship between prevalence and perceptions of severity and noticeability, finding that failures rated as more severe are considered harder to notice, and that prior experience with a failure is associated with greater noticeability. Finally, we assess the maturity of research on each failure and identify commonly encountered failures that have received little attention (e.g., agents running without making progress). Our findings inform opportunities to make delegation easier for users to oversee and better studied by the research community.

OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing mental health care through applications in screening, risk prediction, clinical decision support, documentation, and patient engagement. While these technologies improve efficiency and access, they also present ethical, clinical, and equity challenges that must be addressed in advanced practice nursing. This review synthesizes contemporary evidence on AI in mental health care and discusses its implications for advanced practice nurses (APNs), focusing on ethical implementation, equitable care, and policy. METHODS: An evidence-informed review of literature from 2019 to 2025 was conducted across various databases, including PubMed, CINAHL, and Google Scholar. The review covered AI applications, ethical considerations, health equity, and governance to identify themes relevant to APN practice. RESULTS: AI can enhance psychiatric assessments and patient engagement when used as a decision-support tool. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, inconsistent performance, privacy concerns, and reliance on AI-generated recommendations persist. Emphasizing AI literacy, competency, and governance is crucial for safe, equitable implementation. CONCLUSION: APNs are well-suited to lead the ethical integration of AI in mental health care by merging evidence-based practice and patient advocacy. Ongoing investment in education, policy, and equitable governance is vital for maximizing AI's benefits while maintaining strong therapeutic relationships and quality care.

documents.abstract: High-risk technical operations in oil and gas facilities and construction projects remain difficult to control because work is temporary, interfaces are fragmented, hazardous energy is frequently introduced or released, and schedule pressure can weaken otherwise mature safety systems. This review examines how safety interventions can be configured so that engineered barriers, work-control verification, competence assurance, contractor governance and leading indicators operate as a connected assurance system rather than as isolated programs. A structured integrative review of peer-reviewed literature published from 2020 to 2025 was undertaken, with emphasis on construction safety, oil and gas safety climate, proactive indicators, digital work controls and sociotechnical risk management. The evidence shows that personal-safety programs are valuable for routine exposure reduction, but they do not by themselves provide credible assurance against low-frequency, high-consequence events. Stronger intervention logic emerges when the control selected is matched to the failure mode: physical barriers for hazardous energy, verified permits and isolations for temporary configuration change, competence controls for judgement-intensive tasks, disclosure mechanisms for weak signals, and governance controls for contractor and schedule interfaces. Leading indicators are most useful when they measure the condition of these controls rather than the volume of safety activity. The review develops an integrated assurance framework and proposes practical indicator families for project and operational settings. The central conclusion is that intervention quality depends less on the number of safety initiatives than on whether each critical control is owned, independently verifiable, time-sensitive and connected to decision authority before exposure escalates.

Artificial intelligence is entering architectural design through generative modelling and data-assisted decision support. In developing countries, most of this work is still carried out by architectural small and medium-sized enterprises with limited resources and uneven digital infrastructure. Existing studies have rarely examined how barriers to AI-driven design are ordered. This paper addresses that gap in Iraq. A literature list of 30 statements was refined by a 15-member Delphi panel into 22 barriers in five dimensions. The measurement model was assessed with partial least squares structural equation modelling on 83 practitioner responses. Interpretive structural modelling and MICMAC analysis then placed the dimensions in hierarchy, and the resulting paths were tested on the same data. Economic and institutional deficiencies occupy the driving level. Technological and data readiness acts as a linking layer, while human and organisational capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four paths were significant, the strongest running from institutional deficiencies to technological readiness. The findings indicate that economic and institutional conditions occupy the driving level in the expert hierarchy, while human capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four adjacent paths implied by that hierarchy were statistically significant in the survey data.

This article highlights the crucial role of clinicians as role models in fostering preventive action within medical education. Role modeling is a powerful mechanism in workplace learning, contributing both to medical students' professional identity formation and to their self-efficacy through observational (vicarious) learning. Rather than learning from a single exemplary physician, medical students construct a “mosaic” of role models, drawing on diverse professionals who each demonstrate different competencies. This underscores the importance of exposing medical students to varied clinical perspectives. Despite the growing importance of prevention—driven by aging populations, increasing multimorbidity, and health inequities—medical students report limited exposure to role models who explicitly demonstrate preventive care. Preventive actions are often underrepresented or remain implicit in daily clinical practice, partly because curative care is prioritized and population-level activities are less visible. Additionally, clinicians may not recognize or articulate their own preventive efforts as role modeling opportunities. To address this gap, the article introduces a framework describing preventive action at both individual and population levels, structured around three steps: identification, intervention, and evaluation. Building on this, it outlines how clinicians can model preventive care effectively using four phases of role model learning: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. Practical strategies include making preventive actions visible, explaining underlying reasoning, creating opportunities for practice, and demonstrating outcomes. The article concludes that deliberate and explicit role modeling of prevention, combined with active student engagement, can strengthen learning and support the integration of preventive care as a core component of medical professionalism.

Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

To examine the cognitive consequences of conversational AI-assisted feedback in complex digital learning environments, this study employed a between-subjects longitudinal field design to investigate how both access to and actual engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback were associated with students' perceived extraneous and germane cognitive load during a five-week business simulation game. Because conversational AI-assisted feedback represents an interactive form of instructional support whose effectiveness depends on learner-related and contextual characteristics, the study further examined the moderating roles of simulation progression (time), intrinsic cognitive load, and metacognitive self-regulation. The findings indicate that regular engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback did not uniformly reduce extraneous cognitive load; rather, its effects depended on learners' intrinsic cognitive load and the progression of the intervention. In contrast, students who regularly engaged with the conversational AI-assisted feedback reported significantly higher germane cognitive load than both students without access to the chatbot and students with access who did not use it. Overall, the findings advance understanding of human-AI interaction by demonstrating that the cognitive effects of conversational AI-assisted feedback are shaped by dynamic patterns of learner engagement, individual learning characteristics, and temporal changes during extended AI-supported learning interventions.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges final-product-only coursework assessment: a polished report or design proposal may no longer show how students used AI, which claims they checked, how they attributed sources and AI contributions, or what they revised. This study examined traceable assessment design as a practical response. Rather than relying on AI detection or broad permission rules, assessment tasks were redesigned to collect evidence of students’ AI use, verification, attribution, feedback-mediated revision, and reflective judgement. Using a multi-cycle action research design with an embedded mixed-methods approach, we studied two professional courses: anatomy and physiology as the main evaluation setting and modern microscopy as a secondary adaptation setting. Data sources included coursework, AI-use statements, verification logs, assessment records, student interviews, teacher redesign logs, and traceability-related process indicators. In the main setting, the redesign class recorded higher cumulative report scores than the comparison class (21.59 vs 17.91/30; mean difference = 3.68, 95% CI [1.80, 5.56], Welch t (63.1) = 3.91, p < 0.001, d = 0.96). Of this difference, 3.29 points (89.4%) were concentrated in the redesign-targeted disclosure/citation, verification, and reflection dimensions, compared with 0.39 points across physiology accuracy and the data/evidence chain. The redesign class also recorded higher scores on a design-aligned ethics-focused assessment (14.53 vs 12.36/20; mean difference = 2.17, 95% CI [1.08, 3.26], Welch t (63.9) = 3.99, p < 0.001, d = 0.98), which was not independent evidence of broader ethical learning. Neither OSPE comparison was statistically significant ( p = 127 and 0.334). Across implementation phases, AI-use statement uptake was 88.2% and 91.2%, and verification-log completeness was 1.44 and 1.74. In microscopy, group report scores across three technically different assignments (7.60, 8.03, and 8.60/10) were interpreted descriptively, not as longitudinal improvement. Traceable assessment thus made students’ documented GenAI use, verification, attribution, and revision more inspectable without establishing improved disciplinary learning.

Demand for mentored undergraduate research, scholarship, and creative inquiry (URSCI) opportunities has grown in tandem with research confirming its benefits. Faculty-driven, hypothesis-testing, discipline-centered URSCI is typical; however, students as partners may also contribute meaningfully to operational enhancement or institutional effectiveness (IE) efforts. Building on a student-staff partnership ideal, we developed a potentially scalable model for student-powered, action-focused URSCI, described here using a reflective case study approach. Student-researchers from multiple majors at a large, public university contributed alongside staff to the Information Technology Division’s generative AI support work through a project assessing how undergraduates experience AI advertising. Here, we focus on the processes and structures entailed and the benefits to student collaborators. We also address areas for future research regarding IE as an emerging arena for partner-based URSCI. The analysis contributes conceptually by broadening the URSCI and thereby the Students-as-Partners framework, revealing how and why IE can and should count as a viable—and meaningful—pedagogical domain.

Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in higher education, but it remains unclear whether factors associated with perceived trustworthiness are also associated with students' intentions to adopt them. Drawing on an extended UTAUT2 framework, this study examines how chatbot-specific attributes are associated with trustworthiness, performance expectancy, and hedonic motivation, and how these appraisals, together with UTAUT2 factors, relate to behavioral intention. Survey data from 604 university students in Vietnam were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that ethics (β = 0.294, p < .001) and design (β = 0.458, p < .001) were positively associated with perceived trustworthiness, while social influence was not. Design and interactivity were positively associated with performance expectancy and hedonic motivation. However, perceived trustworthiness (β = 0.043, p = .153), hedonic motivation, and effort expectancy were not significantly associated with behavioral intention. Instead, behavioral intention was most strongly associated with price value (β = 0.408, p < .001), performance expectancy (β = 0.281, p < .001), social influence, and facilitating conditions, and was strongly associated with students' self-reported continued-use tendency (β = 0.754, p < .001). Perceived trustworthiness was not independently associated with behavioral intention in the present model, whereas price value and performance expectancy showed the largest positive associations with intention. This pattern highlights the value of considering trustworthiness alongside instrumental, social, and institutional evaluations when explaining AI-chatbot adoption. The study extends UTAUT2 by integrating these adoption evaluations with an assurance-oriented appraisal of the AI system.

documents.abstract: This study investigates the use of generative AI to support formative assessment through machine-generated reviews of peer reviews (meta-feedback) in graduate online courses in a public university in the United States. Drawing on Systemic Functional Linguistics and Appraisal Theory, we analyzed 120 meta-reviews to explore how generative AI feedback constructs meaning across ideational, interpersonal, and textual dimensions. The findings suggest that generative AI can approximate key rhetorical and relational features of effective human feedback, offering directive clarity while also maintaining a supportive stance. The reviews analyzed demonstrated a balance of praise and constructive critique, alignment with rubric expectations, and structured staging that foregrounded student agency. By modeling these qualities, AI meta-feedback has the potential to scaffold feedback literacy and enhance leaners’ engagement with peer review. We conclude that calibrated AI, when embedded in thoughtfully designed workflows, can contribute to hybrid human–AI feedback ecosystems, while also requiring critical attention to its limitations and contextual adaptation in educational practice.

Recent advances in generative AI have enabled assistants to generate increasingly sophisticated executable unit tests. However, novices may accept these outputs without independently identifying what to test, evaluating test-suite completeness, or verifying correctness, potentially limiting opportunities to develop essential testing skills. Although prior work has explored AI-assisted test generation and feedback-oriented programming tutors, little is known about whether AI can support novices' testing practices without generating tests for them. To investigate this, we introduce TestCompass, a generative AI tutor that provides targeted feedback on weaknesses in students' test suites without generating executable tests. In a classroom study with 18 students, we compared TestCompass with a general AI assistant across two Java unit-testing tasks, examining students' testing behaviors, test-suite quality, and subjective experiences. We found that participants using the general-purpose AI assistant produced more tests, whereas TestCompass participants spent more time developing and verifying tests themselves. However, most test-suite quality measures were comparable between conditions, and TestCompass participants achieved similar requirement coverage with significantly fewer test methods ($p=0.012$) in one task. Neither group reported short-term improvements in perceived testing knowledge or confidence. These findings suggest that feedback-oriented AI can support meaningful testing outcomes while preserving opportunities for hands-on testing practice, offering a complementary approach to AI-assisted testing education.

documents.abstract: There are different levels of transparency for LLMs: open weights, open data, and/or open pipeline. Recently, more interest has emerged in fully transparent LLMs, i.e., LLMs with fully open weights, data, and training pipeline. Drawing analogies to other fields such as software security, it is often believed that increasing transparency inherently increases the security and trustworthiness of the LLM. However, we argue that such claims need to be critically re-evaluated in the context of LLMs. In this paper, we analyze the impact of transparency on LLM security and trustworthiness by reviewing the relevant literature. Our core findings are that, due to the limited reproducibility of LLM pipelines, in practice, users cannot verify the correspondence between open weights and the associated open data and pipeline. Thus, in order to trust a model, users still need to trust that developers acted honestly, reducing the benefits over models that provide less "transparency". Moreover, we find that even when LLMs are fully transparent and trusted, this openness can favor adversaries. Open weights in particular, but also open data and pipelines, can increase the success rate of attacks. Although the same mechanisms can be used to improve the model and protect it against attacks, the current lack of robust lightweight mechanisms to patch LLM vulnerabilities limits the benefits of openness at this time. We note that our analysis is based on current LLM capabilities and analysis tools, and that future developments may require a re-evaluation of these points.

Higher education institutions have adopted artificial intelligence (AI) tools for proctoring, writing detection, student-success prediction, and student support at a pace that has outrun the ethical frameworks meant to govern them. Institutional AI policy has largely borrowed the fairness, accountability, and transparency vocabulary of commercial AI ethics, supplemented by an academic integrity frame focused on student misuse. Empirical studies document harms these frames are poorly equipped to register: automated proctoring that flags Black students and students with darker skin tones at higher rates, AI-text detectors that misclassify non-native English writing as machine-generated, and student-success models that are less accurate for racially minoritized students. This conceptual article introduces the Jones AI Ethics Framework for institutional use. The framework derives five components (Attentiveness, Responsibility, Competence, Responsiveness, and Trust) from Tronto's phases of care and operationalizes each through a corresponding domain of the Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies (MSJCC) and is positioned alongside UNESCO's (2021) Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. The article describes how the framework was developed, specifies its contribution relative to existing care-ethics scholarship on AI, and applies it to two evidence-informed illustrative scenarios: algorithmic proctoring and AI-assisted writing detection. Five recommendations for faculty governance bodies, academic leaders, student affairs professionals, and faculty developers are each mapped to the framework's components. Limitations include the framework's conceptual status, its origin in counselor education, and the need for empirical validation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), into teacher education represents a transformative yet contested development. This article examines the capabilities and biases of LLMs when applied to two critical domains in teacher preparation: situational judgment tests (SJTs) for assessing professional knowledge, and pedagogical decision-making in classroom contexts. Drawing on recent empirical research, we find that LLMs demonstrate significant promise in generating SJT items with psychometric properties comparable to expert-developed assessments, while substantially reducing development time and resource costs. However, LLMs also exhibit systematic biases—including racial, gender, and socioeconomic biases—when evaluating teaching scenarios and generating educational content. These biases manifest across multiple modalities, from text-based evaluations to vision-language models processing classroom imagery. We synthesize findings on LLM capabilities in automated scenario generation, response analysis, and simulation-based training, while critically examining the ethical implications of algorithmic bias in teacher evaluation. The article concludes with recommendations for responsible integration, emphasizing the necessity of human oversight, critical digital pedagogy, and continuous bias auditing in teacher education programs.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explores how pre-service English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers used three Generative AI (GenAI) tools, ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek, while planning and teaching lessons. Drawing on ecological model of teacher agency, it examines how perceived limitations of these tools were associated with different forms of teacher agency, and whether the limitations associated with each form varied across tools. Using a qualitative case study design, the study draws on 58 participants’ reflective essays and observations of 13 classroom lessons. Findings reveal three forms of agency: recontextualizing (adapting generic AI content locally), substitutive (rejecting and replacing impractical suggestions), and improvisational (spontaneous in-class adjustments), each associated with different types of limitations. As a conceptual contribution, the study proposes a three-part typology of teacher agency based on the chordal triad model, and offers recommendations for EFL teacher education, highlighting the need for critical AI literacy and context-sensitive use of multiple GenAI tools.

Evaluating human-AI co-design requires testing whether coding agents can translate real users' multimodal requests into working application revisions. We introduce Co-Design Bench, a reference-free benchmark of 273 tasks curated from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real user coding sessions. Its two tracks, Multimodal Editing (ME) and Repository Editing (RE), cover localized edits with optional image, audio, video, or document inputs and coordinated repository revisions. Tasks span three capability dimensions: Grounded Understanding, UI Transformation, and Functional Implementation. The tasks pair normalized requests and runnable pre-edit applications with 2,331 hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria. Our judge-then-refute protocol grades criteria using source and browser evidence, challenges positive verdicts with a separate LLM verifier, and audits visual and interaction claims without gold code or target screenshots. Under a shared agentic harness, the strongest of ten model endpoints passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. Co-Design Bench provides a testbed for studying the gap between partial requirement satisfaction and complete task success under agentic execution for real-user application revisions.

Abstract This study examines how online Spanish language coaches, that is, trained native speakers who facilitate authentic conversational practice, perceive and use artificial intelligence (AI) in virtual language teaching. While previous research has predominantly focused on classroom teachers, we use a mixed‐methods design that includes a questionnaire and open‐ended responses from 96 coaches based in 15 Spanish‐speaking countries. We examine their familiarity with AI, attitudes toward its use, and views on how it may complement human interaction in language learning. Coaches see clear benefits in using AI for lesson planning, personalization, and idea generation, but they also express concerns about data privacy and ethics, misinformation, reduced critical thinking, and the loss of emotional connection and cultural authenticity. Regression analyses show that familiarity with AI and comfort using it are the strongest predictors of perceived usefulness and willingness to integrate this technology into practice. The findings suggest that professional development should strengthen AI literacy while preserving the interpersonal and intercultural dimensions of language learning. Clear institutional guidance is also needed on AI use and pedagogical approaches that integrate AI without diminishing meaningful human interaction.

Artificial intelligence tools for conversation, programming and speech are usually built and used in isolation, which forces users to carry context manually from one tool to another. This paper presents the COLLABRO AI Ecosystem, a multi-agent platform that unifies conversational assistance, autonomous software engineering and audio intelligence within a single coordinated architecture. Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques are used to interpret user input, infer intent and decompose goals into tasks. An orchestrator agent routes these tasks to specialised agents for dialogue, code understanding, generation and debugging, and speech and audio analysis. A shared context store lets the agents maintain a unified understanding of the user’s goal, exchange intermediate artefacts and improve through feedback. A governance layer embeds data privacy, transparency and responsible automation into every agent interaction. We describe the architecture, the coordination and routing workflow, candidate implementation techniques and the ethical safeguards, and we propose an evaluation protocol with per-agent and cross-agent metrics. The modular design supports software development, enterprise automation, content creation and accessibility applications. This paper reports design and methodology; no quantitative performance results are claimed, and measured evaluation is identified as future work.

Human-robot interaction requires intuitive, efficient, and affordable interfaces for real-world deployment. This work presents a cost-effective comparative study of three interaction modalities such as gesture, voice, and mouse using the ISO 9241-9 pointing task. Twenty participants performed repeated trials in both controlled indoor and uncontrolled outdoor environments. Movement time was analyzed using Fitts’ Law, while cognitive workload and usability were evaluated using NASA-TLX and the System Usability Score. Results show a significant effect of modality on performance, where mouse achieved the lowest movement time, gesture demonstrated comparable performance with no significant difference, and voice exhibited significantly higher delays. Subjective analysis indicates lower workload for mouse, while usability scores remain high across all modalities. Environmental conditions did not significantly affect performance. The findings highlight gesture as a low-cost and touch-less alternative suitable for human-robot interaction, particularly in accessibility-focused and real-world scenarios where conventional input devices are not feasible.

The integration of contextual AI coding assistants, such as GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT, promises productivity gains, yet their adoption depends on complex human factors. This mixed-methods study examines how professional developers perceive, adopt, and integrate these tools, with a focus on experience-related differences. Guided by UTAUT2 and trustin-automation theory, we surveyed 219 developers across four experience tiers and interviewed 14 practitioners. Adoption intentions were associated less with perceived ease of use than with trust calibration centered on output quality. Active verification and strategic integration were positively associated with technical friction, suggesting an exposure effect. Although core perceptions were similar across experience levels, mid-career developers reported stronger performance motivation and friction sensitivity, while senior developers used more refined friction-management strategies. We propose the Trust-Calibration Adoption Framework, extending UTAUT2 by positioning output trustworthiness and experiential learning as central mechanisms. The exploratory findings require replication.

Introduction Teacher autonomy support is associated with adolescent intrinsic motivation, but the shared classroom context is often omitted from analyses. Drawing on self-determination theory and achievement goal theory, this study examined indirect associations through autonomy, competence and relatedness need satisfaction and their moderation by classroom motivational climate. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 2,634 students in 72 secondary-school classes across grades 7–12. A two-level structural equation model with random slopes separated within-class and between-class pathways. Measurement invariance was evaluated across three grade bands. Indirect effects and pairwise contrasts were assessed using 20,000 Monte Carlo draws, and mastery and performance climates were tested as cross-level moderators. Results Scalar measurement invariance supported pooling the grade bands. All three indirect effects were positive at both levels. Within-class estimates through autonomy, competence and relatedness were 0.148, 0.102 and 0.068, respectively; between-class estimates were 0.256, 0.167 and 0.154. Explained variance in intrinsic motivation was 31% within classes and 47% between classes. Pairwise contrasts favored autonomy over the other needs, with weaker evidence for its advantage over competence; competence and relatedness were not statistically distinguishable. The between-class joint equality test was borderline. Mastery climate strengthened the first-stage autonomy and competence paths, whereas performance climate weakened them. Neither moderator was significant for the relatedness path. Discussion The findings support distinguishing individual perceptions from shared classroom conditions when studying autonomy-supportive teaching. Classroom climate may help explain variation in the associations between perceived support, need satisfaction and intrinsic motivation. Because the study was cross-sectional and relied on student self-report, the estimated indirect pathways do not establish causal or temporal ordering.

High-reliable organizing (HRO) has long been associated with how organizations sustain reliable performance under conditions of complexity, uncertainty, and change. While Mindful Organizing (MO), and Resilience Engineering (RE) have generated important theoretical insights, guidance on how organizations can cultivate HRO in everyday organizing remains fragmented. This conceptual essay develops a holistic perspective that positions HRO as an ongoing accomplishment rather than a fixed organizational capability or the outcome of implementing isolated concepts. Through a systematic comparison of the five established MO processes and the four resilience potentials, we show how the two perspectives can be related while preserving their distinct analytical orientations. MO focuses on the collective organizing through which people notice, interpret, coordinate, and respond to emerging situations, while RE emphasizes organizational potentials to monitor, respond, anticipate, and learn under changing conditions. Building on this synthesis, we develop the holistic framework of HRO, identify two additional organizing processes— preoccupation with things that go right and self-awareness —and develop an approach to cultivating and operationalizing HRO through collaborative inquiry, driving forces, and situated practices. Rather than prescribing predefined practices, we argue that organizations can cultivate mindsets and directions of attention that guide how established concepts are translated to context-sensitive action while remaining grounded in the scientific foundations of HRO, MO, and RE. The essay contributes a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding and cultivating high-reliable organizing as an ongoing accomplishment in complex sociotechnical systems.

Objectives: This paper examines a central tension within Industry 4.0. Digitalisation can improve efficiency, monitoring capacity and decision making, but it also creates vulnerabilities linked to digital system failures, cyber incidents and algorithmic bias. The study analyses how these risks condition sustainable and resilient digital transformation in industrial environments and why they are relevant to smart cities. Prior work: The paper builds on research on Industry 4.0, digital transformation and productivity, together with studies on cyber physical systems, smart city security, Internet of Things (IoT) vulnerabilities, artificial intelligence (AI) enabled cyber defence and algorithmic governance. It connects these strands to move beyond technical performance and cybersecurity alone. Approach: The study follows a conceptual and analytical approach, supported by selected secondary evidence from Spain and the European context. Spain provides a contextual empirical anchor for illustrating the operational and social relevance of cyber risk, while the European framework supports the analysis of cybersecurity, algorithmic transparency, human oversight and AI governance. Results: The analysis shows that Industry 4.0 should not be assessed only through automation, efficiency or productivity gains. Its sustainability also depends on resilient digital infrastructures and on the governance conditions under which algorithmic systems are deployed. Under opacity, scale and limited accountability, such systems may amplify hidden biases and generate persistent harms in workforce management, supplier selection and investment allocation. Implications: The findings are relevant for researchers, policy makers and practitioners involved in smart industry and smart city strategies, as they stress the need to align innovation with resilience, accountability and organisational trust. Value: The paper contributes an integrated framework linking cyber resilience, algorithmic governance and social sustainability, showing that sustainable digital transformation requires both resilient infrastructures and accountable automated decisions.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is routinely described as a knowledge technology. This paper argues that the description misplaces a boundary Hayek drew in 1945, between “scientific knowledge”—codifiable, statistical, articulable—and “knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place.” Kiesling (2015) reconstructs part of the latter as the contextual knowledge problem: knowledge that does not exist outside the interaction producing it, as against the complexity problem of aggregating knowledge that exists dispersed but can in principle be codified. The reconstruction is interpretive and identifies a generative subset of Hayek’s category rather than its whole content; much of the remainder is knowledge agents already possess, and AI dissolves a good deal of it. The argument is not that machine systems cannot discover novel alternatives, nor that their search spaces are closed; both are conceded. It is that discovering means does not originate the ultimate ends by reference to which alternatives acquire economic significance, and that current systems receive those ends rather than constituting them. Under a Misesian account of evaluative agency—a premise the paper declares rather than derives—better aggregation, prediction and optimisation therefore cannot by themselves resolve the generative subset, so neither Polanyian tacit knowledge in large language models nor microstructure price discovery by high-frequency traders reaches it. The taxonomy is applied at three levels—the data pipeline, the tacit-knowledge debate, and the institutional conditions of price generation—as three applications of one classification rather than three independent demonstrations. Its products are a set of operational tests, none of which has been run and which are here read against a published Q-learning pricing architecture, and a criterion distinguishing context-preserving from context-suppressing deployment at the level of the market.

Objectives: This study examined dental hygiene students' perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted instruction and the factors influencing their satisfaction with such classes. Methods: A self-administered questionnaire was completed by 80 dental hygiene students who participated in an AI-assisted course. The survey evaluated AI usability, the perceived usefulness of learning activities, learning outcomes, and overall class satisfaction. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, and a hierarchical multiple regression analysis. Results: The mean scores for AI usability and perceived usefulness for learning activities were 4.30 and 4.23, respectively. Among the learning outcomes, collaborative competency received the highest mean score of 4.08, followed by academic achievement at 3.91 and learning motivation and self-efficacy at 3.85. The mean class satisfaction score was 3.76. Students who demonstrated higher AI competency, academic achievement, expected course grades, teamwork, and learning participation reported significantly greater AI usability, perceived usefulness of learning activities, learning outcomes, and class satisfaction (p<0.001). The results of the regression analysis showed that learning outcomes (β=0.381, p<0.001) were the most influential factor on class satisfaction, and academic achievement (β=0.289, p<0.001) and AI competency (β=0.193, p=0.013) were also identified as related factors. Conclusions: These findings indicate that dental hygiene students hold positive perceptions of AI-assisted classes. Importantly, learning outcomes emerge as critical determinants of class satisfaction. Therefore, AI-assisted education should extend beyond the mere introduction of AI tools by enhancing AI literacy and integrating AI thoughtfully into instructional design.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in higher education. Yet educators often adopt it more slowly and cautiously than students, and generic guidance rarely translates into changes in teaching or assessment practice. We designed a short, hands-on, pedagogy-first workshop in which life-science educators work with their own course materials, intended to increase confidence in pedagogically informed AI use and prompt concrete changes to course design, teaching and assessment. However, this is an exploratory feasibility and specification report; therefore, the evaluation was not designed to test that intention. Here we describe the design of a transferable three-session FEBS Education and Training Academy module, organised around the PICRAT (Passive-Interactive-Creative/Replace-Amplify-Transform) framework, a four-element prompt structure and studio-style application to participants' own teaching artefacts, and evaluate it using matched pre/post surveys, anonymous after-session feedback and an online follow-up meeting. Thirty-four educators from 14 countries attended; 21 completed the pre-workshop and 13 the post-workshop survey (12 matched). Among the 12 respondents who completed both surveys, the proportion reporting high confidence rose by the same margin, 4 of 12, in each of the five practical domains. Ten of 13 follow-up respondents reported implementing at least one idea and while views of AI as beneficial were already positive and changed little, agreement that AI poses significant risks to academic integrity fell. These participant-reported, uncontrolled findings should be read as evidence of feasibility and perceived usefulness rather than causal impact.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in early-stage industrial design. It can quickly produce design concepts with strong visual expressiveness. However, these concepts often lack explicit dimensional parameters, material specifications, manufacturing routes, assembly definitions, and structural details. This creates considerable uncertainty for early manufacturability review. Some visual features in concept images may introduce manufacturing, assembly, or maintenance risks. At the same time, these features may also carry design intent related to appearance, functional recognition, interaction cues, or user experience. To address this issue, this study proposes Intent-Sensitive Manufacturability Review (ISMR). ISMR is a human-centered review framework that treats design intent as a soft constraint in early manufacturability review. It organizes visual cues, manufacturability risks, design-intent interpretation, potential intent loss, and required evidence for further verification in a structured manner. The proposed method is compared with an ordinary large language model (LLM)-based review and a traditional Design for Manufacturing (DFM) checklist-based review. The evaluation results show that ISMR performs more prominently in feature specificity and intent sensitivity. It can connect review issues more clearly with visible features in concept images. It also maintains attention to potential design intent when engineering risks are raised. Therefore, ISMR can serve as a useful complement to open-ended LLM review and checklist-based manufacturability review. It provides structured and intent-sensitive support for early design--engineering communication around AI-generated design concepts.

Given the importance of experiencing fulfilling and productive workdays, scholars have focused on ways to boost employees' daily engagement and performance, suggesting this may be accomplished by increasing meaningfulness of their work tasks. However, an alternative approach may be needed in multifaceted work contexts where employees need to complete sets of varied tasks each day, including tasks that lack meaningfulness. To address this issue, we integrate the workday design perspective with research on residual engagement to examine implications of strategically sequencing tasks in terms of their meaningfulness. We theorize that because of a process we refer to as engagement cascade, performing the day's most highly meaningful tasks earlier and in a concentrated manner will tend to produce higher levels of daily engagement relative to sequences in which the most highly meaningful tasks occur later or are disbursed. We use agent-based modeling to formalize the engagement cascade process and generate specific predictions regarding how daily engagement is impacted by different task meaningfulness sequences. Findings from an intensive longitudinal design study with National Aeronautics and Space Administration and Russian Space Agency crew members (Study 1), an experience sampling field experiment with full-time employees (Study 2), and two controlled laboratory experiments with undergraduates (Study 3 and Supplement to Study 3) provide support for our hypotheses. Specifically, the decreasing task meaningfulness sequence engendered higher levels of daily engagement and, in turn, daily performance, relative to the increasing, inverted U-shaped, and U-shaped sequences. Designing Learning That Adapts presents a practical framework for adaptive, scenario-based learning that can be applied across classrooms, e-learning platforms and AI-supported education. Drawing on established learning science, instructional design practice and the questions raised by more than a decade of e-learning product work, the paper sets out principles for shaping learning around the learner's goal, starting point, prior knowledge and preferred ways of learning, and for choosing the right mode (text, voice, video, interaction and dialogue) for each task. It frames adaptive and scenario-based approaches as design practices to be observed, tested and revised rather than as proven efficacy claims, and offers a structured way for educators, platform teams and workplace learning designers to apply these ideas in their own contexts. This is a practitioner framework and does not report an empirical efficacy study.

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of artificial intelligence tools into higher education has created a critical paradox: students engage with AI daily yet rarely develop the skills to evaluate, question, or challenge AI-generated content. This paper presents the Cognitive Bridge methodology — a pedagogical framework developed and implemented at the National Polytechnic University of Armenia (NPUA) over nearly two years of iterative research and classroom practice (2024– 2026) — designed to transform AI from a passive answer-generator into an active cognitive challenge for engineering students. Grounded in Bloom's Revised Taxonomy and Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), the methodology positions AI as a deliberately imperfect cognitive partner whose errors and limitations become the productive substance of learning. Over a four-week quasi-experimental intervention involving approximately 150 engineering students, participants progressed from intuitive AI use (Week 1 baseline) through guided error-detection and critical questioning (Weeks 2–3) to independent AI auditing (Week 4). Findings are supported by a parallel anonymous survey of N=149 engineering students on AI ethics awareness, revealing moderate AI literacy (Q10: M=3.29/5; Q11: M=3.34/5) alongside critically low knowledge of the EU AI Act (Q12: M=2.27/5). Qualitative thematic analysis identified three dominant themes: AI dependency as the primary ethical concern, university responsibility for structured instruction, and spontaneous student recognition of the Cognitive Bridge instruction in anonymous surveys. Results suggest that structured, longitudinal AI-challenge pedagogy significantly develops critical thinking, verification habits, and ethical awareness, offering a scalable, low-cost model applicable across diverse institutional contexts.

documents.abstract: This article examines how generative artificial intelligence (AI) assistants can strengthen Lean Six Sigma (LSS) execution across every phase of the Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control (DMAIC) methodology. The objective is to give LSS practitioners field-tested patterns, quantified cycle-time data, and a governance framework for integrating AI assistants into quality-improvement projects without compromising methodological rigor. The investigation draws on recent industry deployments using Anthropic’s Claude assistant and a construct called skills: versioned playbooks that bundle written instructions, scripts, reference data, and validation rules into reusable artifacts. Methods include direct measurement of cycle-time deltas across Define, Measure, and Control tasks; four worked Analyze-phase examples spanning hypothesis testing, Measurement System Analysis, Statistical Process Control, and regression interpretation; and analysis of a multi-skill portfolio deployed at a small aviation services client. Results demonstrate substantial efficiency gains: project-charter drafting time fell from 90 to 120 minutes to roughly 6 minutes; monthly payroll consolidation fell from 90 minutes to under 30 seconds (a 99.4 percent reduction) with the first-pass error rate dropping to zero; cross-system benefits reconciliation fell from 4 hours to under 60 seconds, with monthly completion improving from 5 of 12 cycles to 12 of 12. The aggregate skills portfolio at one client achieved approximately 84 hours of administrative cycle-time savings per year. The article identifies six required governance controls (human review, version control, controlled prompts, sensitive-data boundaries, hallucination mitigation, and auditability) and aligns them with ISO 9001: 2015 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The conclusion is that generative AI does not alter DMAIC methodology; it lowers the cost of executing each phase well, expanding the share of LSS that is practiced in fact rather than only in theory. The findings support Master Black Belts and quality champions in deliberately piloting AI-enabled tooling, prioritizing Control-phase tasks first, and treating skill development as a formal deliverable with version control, ownership, and quality gates.

documents.abstract: EPT E INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFIOS E POSSIBILIDADES PARA A FORMAÇÃO DE PROFISSIONAIS NA ERA DIGITAL. VOCATIONAL AND TECHNOLOGICAL EDUCATION AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: CHALLENGES AND POSSIBILITIES FOR PROFESSIONAL TRAINING IN THE DIGITAL AGE. EDUCACIÓN PROFESIONAL Y TECNOLÓGICA E INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFÍOS Y POSIBILIDADES PARA LA FORMACIÓN DE PROFESIONALES EN LA ERA DIGITAL. Gabriel Nascimento de Carvalho Simone Helen Drumond Ischkanian Gladys Nogueira Cabral Celine Maria de Sousa Azevedo Silvana Nascimento de Carvalho Sygride Nascimento de Carvalho Sandro Garabed Ischkanian RESUMO A Educação Profissional e Tecnológica (EPT) enfrenta desafios relacionados à incorporação da inteligência artificial nos processos de ensino e aprendizagem, na organização curricular e no desenvolvimento de competências necessárias ao mundo do trabalho. A expansão das tecnologias digitais demanda reflexões sobre as possibilidades de inovação pedagógica, a preparação dos docentes, a formação crítica dos estudantes e as implicações éticas do uso de sistemas inteligentes. Diante desse cenário, estabelece-se como problema de pesquisa: de que maneira a inteligência artificial pode contribuir para a formação de profissionais na EPT, considerando as exigências da transformação digital e os desafios de sua implementação educacional? O objetivo geral consiste em analisar os desafios e as possibilidades da integração da inteligência artificial à formação profissional, com atenção às competências técnicas, digitais, críticas e éticas requeridas na contemporaneidade. Metodologicamente, propõe-se uma pesquisa qualitativa, de caráter exploratório e descritivo, desenvolvida por meio de revisão bibliográfica e análise documental de publicações científicas e documentos institucionais pertinentes à temática. A análise permite discutir possibilidades de personalização da aprendizagem, apoio às atividades pedagógicas, simulação de situações profissionais e aproximação entre educação e transformações tecnológicas. Também evidencia desafios relativos à infraestrutura, à formação docente, à proteção de dados, aos vieses algorítmicos e às desigualdades de acesso. Conclui-se que a integração da inteligência artificial à EPT requer planejamento pedagógico, formação continuada e princípios éticos, de modo a articular inovação tecnológica, inclusão educacional e desenvolvimento humano na preparação dos profissionais para a era digital. Palavras-chave: Educação profissional e tecnológica; inteligência artificial; formação profissional; competências digitais. ABSTRACT Professional and Technological Education (PTE) faces challenges related to the incorporation of artificial intelligence into teaching and learning processes, curriculum organization, and the development of skills required in the world of work. The expansion of digital technologies calls for reflection on the possibilities of pedagogical innovation, teacher preparation, students’ critical development, and the ethical implications of using intelligent systems. Against this background, the research problem is formulated as follows: how can artificial intelligence contribute to professional training in PTE, considering the demands of digital transformation and the challenges of its educational implementation? The general objective is to analyze the challenges and possibilities of integrating artificial intelligence into professional education, focusing on the technical, digital, critical, and ethical competencies required in contemporary society. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive approach, based on a literature review and documentary analysis of scientific publications and institutional documents relevant to the topic. The analysis discusses opportunities for personalized learning, support for pedagogical activities, simulation of professional situations, and closer alignment between education and technological change. It also identifies challenges involving infrastructure, teacher training, data protection, algorithmic bias, and unequal access. The study concludes that integrating artificial intelligence into PTE requires pedagogical planning, continuing professional development, and ethical principles to connect technological innovation, educational inclusion, and human development in preparing professionals for the digital age. Keywords: Professional and technological education; artificial intelligence; professional training; digital competencies. RESUMEN La Educación Profesional y Tecnológica (EPT) enfrenta desafíos relacionados con la incorporación de la inteligencia artificial en los procesos de enseñanza y aprendizaje, la organización curricular y el desarrollo de competencias necesarias para el mundo laboral. La expansión de las tecnologías digitales exige reflexionar sobre las posibilidades de innovación pedagógica, la preparación del profesorado, el desarrollo del pensamiento crítico del alumnado y las implicaciones éticas del uso de sistemas inteligentes. Ante este escenario, se plantea el siguiente problema de investigación: ¿de qué manera puede contribuir la inteligencia artificial a la formación de profesionales en la EPT, considerando las exigencias de la transformación digital y los desafíos de su implementación educativa? El objetivo general consiste en analizar los desafíos y las posibilidades de integrar la inteligencia artificial en la formación profesional, prestando atención a las competencias técnicas, digitales, críticas y éticas requeridas en la sociedad contemporánea. Metodológicamente, se propone una investigación cualitativa, de carácter exploratorio y descriptivo, basada en una revisión bibliográfica y un análisis documental de publicaciones científicas y documentos institucionales pertinentes. El análisis permite examinar las posibilidades de personalizar el aprendizaje, apoyar las actividades pedagógicas, simular situaciones profesionales y fortalecer la articulación entre educación y transformaciones tecnológicas. También identifica desafíos relacionados con la infraestructura, la formación docente, la protección de datos, los sesgos algorítmicos y las desigualdades de acceso. Se concluye que la integración de la inteligencia artificial en la EPT requiere planificación pedagógica, formación continua y principios éticos que articulen innovación tecnológica, inclusión educativa y desarrollo humano en la preparación de profesionales para la era digital.
